$comment: What the Gin (Go) reference implementation claims, and the evidence for every requirement not proven by a conformance case. Checked by apps/playground-gin/test/conformance/report.test.ts; rendered to docs/conformance-gin.md.
title: Gin (Go) reference implementation

supports.title: Gin 1.12 + Go (a Go port of the core)
PostgreSQL via pgx (the same migration SQL as the TypeScript apps; a small migration runner)
Vue 3 (generated as client/ next to the Go server in server/; browser-tested against the Go server)
React (generated as client/ next to the Go server in server/; browser-tested against the Go server)

limitations: Gin supports PostgreSQL and the in-memory store only. MySQL, SQLite and MongoDB are not implemented for Go.

`selfauth add` does not work on existing Go projects (new projects only). A Vue or React frontend is generated as `client/` next to the Go server in `server/`, and the browser spec runs against the Go server on the in-memory store.

PostgreSQL is claimed at authorization level, not production: the production profile has not been reviewed for the Go adapter (pool sizing, statement timeouts, behaviour under replica failover were chosen and tested, not audited).
The in-memory store loses data on restart and keeps rate limits per process. It is capped at authorization level and is not for production.
The migration runner does not detect destructive statements (unlike `selfauth db plan` for Prisma projects): read every migration before applying it.

Two implementations of the core now exist. The conformance suite detects drift in the behaviour it covers; behaviour outside the cases is covered by the Go unit tests and review. Known differences (trusted proxies as a list only, simple case folding of email addresses, trailing slashes) are listed in apps/playground-gin/README.md.
Email and password only. No OAuth, social login, MFA or passkeys (optional capabilities, not built).
The mailer is a stub: you must implement NewMailer before production, and the server refuses to start in production without one.
Production-profile status is not claimed for Gin: the adapter has had no review except its author's. The sign-offs below are self-assessed, and no independent security audit has been done.

signoffs.finding: docs/data-retention.md lists what deletion clears, deletes, revokes and keeps, how long, and how to purge it; checked against deleteUser in the Go core (internal/auth/service.go) and the migration SQL, which is the same schema as the TypeScript apps.
The store contract suite makes the role link fail and asserts no user or credential remains; it runs against the in-memory and the PostgreSQL store, where creation is one transaction.
A test counts Argon2 evaluations: a login for an account that does not exist costs exactly as many as a login with a wrong password.
Login calls VerifyDummy on the no-user path and has no early return before password verification.
A test counts Argon2 evaluations: registering an address that already has an account costs the same as a new one.
Register hashes the password before looking the email up, so every path costs the same.

The example route is guarded and tested anonymously; routes on ProtectedRoutes deny every request that no guard allows (tested). Unlike the TypeScript apps there is no test that fails on any unguarded route in application code: that remains a review item.
Config validation rejects malformed permission names (the Go configuration is validated at start-up with the specification's bounds).
Config validation rejects project permissions using the reserved 'auth.' prefix.
Config validation rejects roles that reference undefined permissions.
RequirePermission with an undefined permission panics when the route is defined.
Role and permission sync is exercised against PostgreSQL and never prunes assignments: a user keeps a role that disappeared from the configuration.
Roles are synchronized by the seed command only; the PostgreSQL store does no sync at startup (the in-memory store is synchronized on start because it holds no data).
CT-IDENT-007 asserts the stored verifier is an Argon2id PHC string.
Hashing is golang.org/x/crypto/argon2 (the Go project's maintained implementation) with IDKey (Argon2id); there is no hand-written implementation, and verification compares in constant time.
A test runs many password hashes at once and answers a request that needs none before they finish; every request is its own goroutine and concurrent hashes are bounded so memory cannot be exhausted.
Config validation rejects minLength below 8.
No setting or code path expires or rotates passwords; the password block of the configuration struct has only length, common-password and hashing keys, and a test rejects an added age key.

Tests assert the verification link carries the token in the fragment (never a query string) and that responses send a no-referrer policy. Rendering email-link pages is the frontend's job (the reference frontends are tested separately).
NewAuth refuses an insecure session cookie and an http base URL when APP_ENV is production.

The Gin backend never redirects: no handler issues a Location header, and trailing-slash and path-fixing redirects are disabled. Redirect handling after sign-in belongs to a frontend, which a Gin project does not generate.
A test sends hostile redirect and next parameters and odd paths and asserts no response is a redirect or carries a Location header.
The security workflow runs gitleaks over the full history on every push and pull request and weekly; the configuration struct has no secret fields.
The configuration is decoded strictly and has no field that holds a secret (a test walks the struct); secrets come from environment variables.
A test asserts the generated .env.example holds placeholders only and .gitignore covers .env.
Tests assert start-up fails without a valid SELFAUTH_APP_BASE_URL, and that token-mode CSRF cannot start without a secret of at least 32 bytes.
Tests assert CSRF secrets under 32 bytes are refused, tokens signed with the previous secret are still accepted, and tokens signed with a dropped secret are refused.
The previous secret is verified but never used to sign, so rotation cannot keep an old key alive.
The Store interface can only append security events (RecordEvent), and no route or service updates or deletes one.
The options that reveal registered emails are off in the default configuration, and sign-in after registration is rejected unless the reveal option is on.
The customization guide describes the revealExistingEmail trade-off.
selfauth doctor warns when revealExistingEmail is enabled in a Gin project's selfauth.config.json.
The deployment guide requires HTTPS and shows the HSTS header; NewAuth and the environment loader refuse an http base URL in production.
A test asserts the unique indexes exist on a fresh database, and the store contract suite shows concurrent registrations of one address create one account.
Migrations are applied and verified on a fresh PostgreSQL schema by the project's migration runner: once, idempotently, with edited migrations refused and concurrent runs serialized.
The application never migrates or seeds at startup; migrations are applied only by the explicit migrate command.
A test migrates a schema that already holds an application table with rows and asserts they are untouched and that every other table is SelfAuth's own (auth_ prefix).
Every error carries a stable code; no Go code matches message text (errors are inspected with errors.As and switched on Code), and the conformance runner branches on error.code.
The configuration is decoded with unknown fields disallowed; tests reject unknown top-level and nested keys.
Unknown keys are rejected, so a secret cannot be added to the config file.
No field in the configuration struct carries a secret.
Out-of-range TTLs, lengths and timeouts are rejected, not clamped.
The store factory rejects a configuration naming a database this adapter does not implement (MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB), and the proxy setting refuses a hop count.
Config validation rejects an unsupported major specVersion.
